name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Wednesday 12 October 1983

clue.text: Slander in accordance with directions.

blocks.note: 'as per' means according to
south-east, two compass directions

explanation.surface: Someone defames another person while claiming to be following instructions.
explanation.walkthrough: AS PER plus SE. 'Directions' looks like orders, but here it means compass points.
explanation.definitionFit: To asperse is to cast damaging, false charges on a person's reputation, a formal verb for defaming.

clue.text: Its purr might suggest a footrest.

indicators.note: the letters only hint at the answer, so they must be rearranged before they spell it

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cat's purring hints that it wants somewhere to put its feet up.
explanation.walkthrough: The rider's foot sits in the stirrup, so it is a footrest of a sort.
explanation.definitionFit: A stirrup is the loop hanging from a saddle in which a rider rests a foot.

clue.text: Preclude honest operators taking part

indicators.note: the answer takes only part of the following words, sitting across them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word and start of the next

explanation.surface: A rule to keep honest businesses out of some deal.
explanation.definitionFit: Estop is a legal term meaning to bar or prevent someone from asserting something.

clue.text: Captain who jumps to it?

definitions.note: a description; the answer is the noun for such a person

blocks.note: first meaning: the master of a boat or leader of a team
second meaning: one who skips, hopping along

explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumps to it' suggests a crew obeying orders; here it is someone skipping. The question mark flags that this sense is invented.
explanation.definitionFit: A skipper is the master of a boat or a team captain, and literally one who skips.

clue.text: Blow for no-side at the theatre?

definitions.text: Blow for no-side at the theatre?

blocks.note: surface reading: in rugby, no-side is the referee's final whistle, the blow that ends play
setter's reading: a stage play about the close of a match, and in fact a Samuel Beckett play

explanation.walkthrough: No-side is the rugby term for full time. The finish of a game, taken literally, is also the title of Beckett's 1957 play, which is why the theatre comes in.
explanation.definitionFit: Endgame is Beckett's play, and its name literally describes the closing stage of a game, which the final whistle signals.

clue.text: A darn good thing.

blocks.note: surface reading: 'darn' as a mild oath, meaning a really good thing
setter's reading: to darn is to mend a hole in a sock, and this is the tool that does it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Darn' poses as a polite swear word; it is the mending stitch.
explanation.definitionFit: A darning needle is a long sewing tool with a large eye used to repair holes in knitted fabric.

clue.text: Dish served up in a tangle

indicators.note: food served up has been prepared, so the letters are reworked like ingredients

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A meal arrives at the table in a muddled mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a tangle' looks like the anagram signal, but it is the fodder; 'served up' does the mixing.
explanation.definitionFit: A galantine is a cold dish of boned, stuffed and pressed meat served in aspic.

clue.text: Runs someone for a long period.

blocks.note: a man is a person
ages means a very long time

explanation.surface: An athlete jogs for hours on end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs' looks like jogging but means directs or operates.
explanation.definitionFit: To manage a business is to run it, in the sense of being in charge.

clue.text: Sustained gaiety when gin, etc, is poured out

definitions.text: when gin, etc, is poured out

blocks.note: first meaning: lasting cheerfulness, high spirits that keep coming

blocks.clueFragment: when gin, etc, is poured out
blocks.note: second meaning: literally, spirits such as gin streaming from a bottle

explanation.walkthrough: The anagram-looking 'poured out' and 'gin' tempt a reshuffle, but the letters do not fit; spirits means both mood and liquor.
explanation.definitionFit: A flow of spirits is an idiom for buoyant, lasting good humour, and literally a stream of hard liquor.

clue.text: Heel in the border.

blocks.note: first meaning: a ship heels over when it tilts to one side
second meaning: the selvage or edge strip of a woven cloth

explanation.walkthrough: 'Heel' suggests a shoe or a scoundrel, but here it is the nautical verb for leaning over.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship that lists leans to one side, the same as heeling, and a list is also an old word for the edging strip of fabric.

clue.text: Bad blood giving rise to sickly sensation.

blocks.note: first meaning: hostility between people
second meaning: read literally, a feeling of being ill

explanation.surface: A feud between two people leaves one of them feeling physically queasy.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is taken once as an idiom for animosity and once word for word as feeling unwell.
explanation.definitionFit: Ill feeling is an idiom for resentment or enmity, exactly what bad blood describes between people.

clue.text: Support for a young animal.

blocks.note: pro means in favour of
a pup is a young dog or seal

explanation.surface: Someone shores up a weak baby animal, or arranges a prop for it.
explanation.walkthrough: PRO plus PUP. 'For' looks like a link word, but it supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To prop up is a phrasal verb meaning to hold something up or keep it from collapsing, so it means support.

clue.text: Spring is near - almost

blocks.note: a spring is a natural source of water, as is a well
nigh is an old word for near

explanation.surface: An announcement that springtime has nearly arrived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' reads as the season, but it is a water source.
explanation.definitionFit: Well-nigh is a slightly old-fashioned adverb meaning very nearly or all but.

clue.text: Fish with a tendency to cause spray.

blocks.note: to spin is to fish with a revolving lure called a spinner
the drift of things is their general tendency or trend

explanation.surface: A fish that is prone to splashing water about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish' looks like a noun but is the verb for angling.
explanation.definitionFit: Spindrift is the fine sea spray blown off wave crests by the wind.

clue.text: Coin freshly minted in Pacific island.

blocks.note: freshly made means new
the guinea was an old British gold coin worth 21 shillings

explanation.surface: A newly struck coin turns up in the Pacific.
explanation.walkthrough: The adjective follows the noun in the clue but comes first in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: New Guinea is the large island north of Australia, in the western Pacific Ocean.

clue.text: Pioneer in putting a tree on the street.

definitions.note: taken as an adjective: pioneering, the earliest

blocks.note: a fir is a conifer
St is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: Someone is first to plant a tree on the road outside.
explanation.walkthrough: FIR is placed before ST, the street sign abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A pioneer is the one who comes before everyone else, the first to do something.

clue.text: Tied or tired, perhaps.

blocks.note: first meaning: a match ending level is a ... game
second meaning: a face looking strained or haggard, often from fatigue

explanation.walkthrough: The two words differ by one letter, which tempts the solver to look for a letter trick; there is none, they are just two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawn match ends level, and a drawn face looks strained and exhausted, hence 'perhaps' for tiredness.

clue.text: Drive over to criticise.

blocks.note: first meaning: to knock someone over with a vehicle
second meaning: to disparage or belittle

explanation.surface: A driver deliberately runs over someone to show disapproval.
explanation.definitionFit: To run down is to hit with a car, and as an idiom it means to speak badly of someone.

clue.text: Birds shot by sporting gentlemen would hardly fit in here.

definitions.text: Birds shot by sporting gentlemen would hardly fit in here.

blocks.note: surface reading: the game bag of grouse or pheasant from a day's shooting
setter's reading: a small bathroom bag for washing things, far too little for a day's haul of game

explanation.walkthrough: The game bag is what shooters fill; this is a much smaller bag holding soap and a flannel. A sponge bag is the British name for a toiletry bag.
explanation.definitionFit: A sponge bag is a small waterproof toiletries pouch, a bag that clearly could not hold a brace of shot birds.

clue.text: She may show the North the way out.

definitions.note: a pronoun standing for a noun: a woman

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for north
egress is a formal word for an exit

explanation.surface: A woman guides northerners towards the exit.
explanation.walkthrough: The word was routine in 1983 but is now dated and offensive. The definition is just 'She', a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: The word was an old term for a black woman, so it stands for 'she' as a female person.

clue.text: Fish-woman takes drink first

blocks.note: ale is beer
a wife is a woman

explanation.surface: A fishwife gets a drink before anything else.
explanation.walkthrough: The drink is placed before the woman. The hyphen in 'Fish-woman' hides that 'Fish' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The alewife is a North American herring-like fish.

clue.text: A council at sea?

blocks.note: taken as written
a board is a governing committee

explanation.surface: A governing committee that is confused or meeting on a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At sea' suggests confused; here it means on a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Aboard means on a ship, which is where someone at sea is.

clue.text: Embarrass by prescribing measure to cure doctor, perhaps.

indicators.note: a doctor prescribing makes up a mixture, so the letters that follow are mixed up

blocks.note: an en is a printer's measure of width
taken as written
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's degree; 'perhaps' because a doctor is one example of a holder

explanation.surface: A doctor is shamed by being prescribed some measure to cure himself.
explanation.walkthrough: Embarrass is used in its old sense of hamper or burden. The parse of the indicator is tentative: EN plus a mix of CURE and MB.
explanation.definitionFit: To encumber is to weigh down or impede, matching the older meaning of embarrass as to hamper someone.

clue.text: Supporter that does tend to go on.

definitions.text: Supporter that does tend to go on.

blocks.clueFragment: Supporter that does tend to go on
blocks.note: surface reading: a fan or backer who talks on and on
setter's reading: a band that holds up a stocking and is put on, worn, round the leg

explanation.walkthrough: 'Go on' suggests talking at length; it means being put on as clothing. The definition is tentative.
explanation.definitionFit: A garter is an elastic band worn round the leg to hold a stocking up, so it supports something.

clue.text: Right ones to take note of spokes.

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right
an ad is a short notice
I is the Roman numeral one, twice over

explanation.surface: The correct people should notice a wheel's spokes.
explanation.walkthrough: The parse is tentative: the letters come in clue order only if the ones take the note in front of them.
explanation.definitionFit: The radii of a circle are lines from the centre to the rim, as the spokes of a wheel are.

clue.text: Head ornament on man in town.

blocks.note: a horn grows from an animal's head
a man is a chess piece, and a castle is one

explanation.surface: A man wearing a hat decoration in the town.
explanation.walkthrough: In chess any piece is a man; the castle (rook) is one. Horncastle is a market town in Lincolnshire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Horncastle is a small market town in Lincolnshire in the east of England.

clue.text: Dead and buried in the fall.

blocks.note: d. is the abbreviation for died or dead in records
RIP, rest in peace, is carved over the buried

explanation.surface: Someone killed and laid in the earth during autumn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The fall' suggests autumn, the American word, but the definition is the verb for liquid falling in drops.
explanation.definitionFit: To drip is to fall in drops, as water does from a tap.

clue.text: How introspective sister may look.

blocks.note: surface reading: a reflective nun gazing into her own soul
setter's reading: a nursing sister looks in on the hospital wards

explanation.walkthrough: A sister is also a senior hospital nurse, who checks the wards; split, the answer reads IN WARDS.
explanation.definitionFit: Inwards means towards the inside, the direction an introspective person turns their thoughts.

clue.text: Hoped to rise from utter despair.

indicators.note: utter here suggests complete chaos, so the following word's letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone tried to lift themselves out of total hopelessness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Utter' looks like an adjective describing despair, but it signals the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: To aspire is to hope or aim for something higher; the Latin root means to breathe towards, rising upward.
